Testimony ofSen. Cameron Reny introducing
LD 144, "An Act to Create a Limited Retail Seafood Harvester Certificate"
before the Joint Standing Committee on Marine Resources
February 6, 2025
Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler, and honorable members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Marine Resources, I am Senator Cameron Reny, and I represent District 13, which includes most of
Lincoln County and the towns of Washington and Windsor. Today, I am presenting LD 144, "An Act
to Create a Limited Retail Seafood Harvester Certificate."
This bill from the Department of Marine Resources will make it easier for shellfish harvesters to sell their harvest without having to shoulder the expense of fixed facilities or run their product through registered dealers. It would allow them to sell their shellfish out of a vehicle, at locations like a farmer's
market. It aims to increase direct sales from aquaculture farmers and shellfish harvesters to the
consumer, thereby increasing availability of fresh and affordable shellfish in Maine. To be clear, this bill only applies to shellstock, or unshucked shellfish, provided by shellfish harvesters themselves.
There will be testimony from the Department and others coming behind me, and I ask that you direct
further technical questions to them.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely,

Cameron Reny
State Senator, District 13
Representing Lincoln County and the towns of Washington and Windsor

10031667:
Testimony in Support of LD 144
An Act to Create a Limited Retail Seafood Harvester Certificate
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Marine Resources February 6, 2025
Honorable Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Marine Resources:
Over one year ago, members of the Shellfish Advisory Council (ShAC) formed a Retail Rules Committee to streamline retail shellfish regulations. The goal of this Committee is to make direct-to-customer sales more accessible to harvesters of different incomes, while reducing time to market, adding safety checks absent from the current system, and providing new opportunities to expand the Maine shellfish industry.
Under current law, shellfish harvesters with retail licenses have two paths to sell their own product to retail customers:
The first requires harvesters to operate and maintain a shellfish dealer facility (at significant expense) -even if shellfish is never stored at this facility and is only re-tagged. This locks many small-scale harvesters out of retail sales, which is a problem poised to worsen in a tight real estate market.
The second path requires harvesters to sell their product to a dealer to then buy back (at a loss) before resale to retail customers. The inefficiency of this system leads to a longer, less safe chain-of-custody and unnecessary expense.
To address these barriers and inefficiencies, the Committee's work focused on finding a safe way to eliminate the requirement that harvesters operate a brick-and-mortar dealer facility. The proposed rule changes would allow harvesters to sell their own product in-state from a vehicle within the strict time and temperature requirements laid out in the state's vibrio control rules. These changes would allow wild harvesters and shellfish farmers of all scales to reach new markets and receive a fair price for their catch.
We discussed the DMR's proposal to create a limited retail seafood harvester certificate at the September 19, 2024 ShAC meeting, where we voted (10-1-1: In favor, opposed, abstention) to express the ShAC's support for this bill to the Commissioner. This support has continued now with LD 144, with the exception of one member. Thank you for your time and consideration of this testimony.
On behalf of the Shellfish Advisory Council: Jessica Gribbon Joyce (Chair), Lewis Pinkham (Vice Chair) & Jordan Kramer (Retail Rules Committee Chair)
183521:
TESTIMONY OF
Kohl Kanwit Department of Marine Resources

The Department of Marine Resources (DMR) is testifying
in Support of
LD 144 An Act to Create a Limited Retail Seafood Harvester Certificate Before the Committee on Marine Resources
Sponsored by Senator Reny Date of Hearing: February 6, 2025

Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Marine
Resources, my name is Kohl Kanwit, Director of the Department of Marine Resources Bureau of Public Health and Aquaculture, and l am testifying on behalf of the Department in support of LD 144. This is a Department bill, and we are grateful to Senator Reny for sponsoring this bill on our behalf.

This bill is the product of a working group of the Shellfish Advisory Council to identify a mechanism to provide additional flexibility in the sale of shellfish while remaining protective of public health. As was explained in the Department's presentation, DMR's Bureau of Bureau of Public Health oversees the application of the National Shellfish Sanitation Program (NSSP) within the State of Maine. This program is implemented internationally by the interstate Shellfish Sanitation Conference (ISSC) in order to keep
molluscan shellfish safe for human consumption. This is accomplished by making sure that a common set of standards are used to classify shellfish growing areas and handle shellfish when they go to
market.

Under the current law, a shellfish harvester can sell shellstock (unshucked shellfish) they have taken,
only as follows:

~

They can sell shellstock they have taken, from their home in the retail trade, except that they

cannot sell oysters from their home during the Vibrio control months (June-October)

~

They can sell shellstock they have taken from a fixed facility that is not their home, if they have

a retail license and an enhanced retail certificate, and meet the requirements for the facility

established in rule. Facilities must meet a number of requirements, including having a

bathroom, hot water, wash down walls, etc., so maintaining a facility increases expenses.

v

They can sell shellstock they have taken to a certified wholesale seafood dealer, who can then

sell it in the wholesale or retail trade.

Shellfish harvesters, and in particular, oyster growers, are looking for additional flexibility in how they
can sell their product directly to the consumer, without having to establish a fixed facility (which is expensive) or run their product through a certified dealer (which also increases their costs). To be
clear, this proposal is a mechanism for them to sell only shellstock the license holder has harvested
themselves.

Through the Shellfish Advisory Council, shellfish harvesters asked for a solution that would allow them to sell their shellfish from a vehicle, at such locations as a farmer's market. The proposed limited retail harvester certificate would create a new opportunity for harvesters to use a vehicle to sell shellstock they have taken from a vehicle without having to involve a certified shellfish dealer in the sale. They will still need to meet requirements for the safe handling of shellstock shellfish established
in rule, but we anticipate it will be less onerous than the requirements associated with a fixed facility.
As you can see from the bill language, this would be implemented by a harvester first obtaining a retail
shellfish license. They would also obtain the new limited retail shellfish harvester certificate, which
would be assigned to a single vehicle. As a point of information, in DMR statutes "vehicle" may include
a watercraft, and we are aware that some harvesters have an interest in using this license associated
with a vessel, rather than a car or truck. The holder would then be authorized to sell, transport and serve in the retail trade and within state limits, shellstock taken by the license holder. The vehicle would be subject to inspection, and the Department would have authority to adopt rules establishing the sanitation and handling requirements of the shellfish.
Thank you for your consideration, and l would be happy to answer any questions you might have.
10032373:
Trey Angera Gouldsboro LD 144
I am writing in opposition to this bill.
There have been an increasing number of reports of vibrio, campylobactor, and other shellfish diseases that impact human health. Our system in Maine is currently based on fixed location dealers/sellers that are inspected and subject to "surprise" inspections. This system protects consumers and the industry as a whole.
This proposal creates a "mobile" dealer license that can be either a car or boat. While the DMR can regulate the standards for these vehicles, how will there be enforcement? How can Marine Patrol or other DMR representatives inspect these vehicles in real time? The answer is they cannot. This proposed bill essentially creates a dealer with an honor system for enforcement which is contrary to current policy and the health of consumers.
This bill should not be approved. If approved, it should be amended to require the license holder to notify the DMR of when and where sales will be conducted so that random and regular inspections can be conducted to preserve public safety.
Thank you.
